name: S1.Diagnose
description: Turn structured performance traces for competitive-programming style solutions into a concise optimization brief that identifies dominant bottlenecks and prescribes abstract refactor directions.

name: S2 Retrieve Operator Budget
description: Meta-skill that, given task context and an operator registry, selects a small, dynamically sized subset of operator skills most likely to improve a competitive-programming style solution (algorithmic and constant-factor optimization). It uses problem features, registry metadata, and global trace statistics to pick and order operators while respecting a budget.

name: S3.Strategize
description: A reusable meta-skill for constructing executable optimization strategies: selecting algorithms, data structures, and implementation tactics; sequencing them into a coherent plan; and adapting the plan under constraints for broad competitive-programming style tasks.

name: S4 Judge Rank Candidate Solutions
description: A reusable meta-skill for ranking multiple candidate competitive-programming solutions (or refactors) by balancing performance upside, correctness risk, and strength of supporting evidence.

name: Fast IOAnd Constant Factor Tuning
description: Optimize I/O and hot-path implementation details without changing asymptotic complexity: switch to fast input/output, remove unnecessary memory operations and branches, simplify arithmetic, and tighten data layout (raw arrays, local state) so existing O(N), O(N log N), or DP algorithms run within strict time limits.
triggers: Algorithmic structure between slow and fast code is identical but slow version uses cin/cout (often mixed with stdio) and fast version uses scanf/printf or custom readers.
Large input/output volume: arrays sized around 1e5–1e6, many testcases, or O(N^2) grids where most time is spent reading or printing rather than computing.
Use of cin/cout without ios::sync_with_stdio(false) and cin.tie(nullptr), or frequent std::endl in loops.
Character-by-character or per-element formatted I/O inside tight loops, especially nested loops.

Heavy string or container usage in hot paths: std::string concatenation in output loops, std::stringstream for int<->string, std::set or std::vector<bool> where small fixed arrays or bitwise ops would suffice.
Full-size memset over large static arrays per testcase when only a prefix is used, or repeated zeroing of big DP tables.
Redundant arithmetic or branching in inner loops: repeated recomputation of the same expression, unnecessary abs() or modulo, complex indexing conversions.
Global overprovisioned buffers (e.g., arrays of size 100000+ for data of size n) and scattered global state instead of compact local arrays or fixed-size small vectors.

Sorting of large arrays of 32‑bit or 64‑bit integers or simple pairs/tuples where only grouping or order by those integers is required, and profiling or reasoning shows std::sort or qsort dominating runtime.

name: Template Preamble Refactor

You are building a reusable competitive-programming library and want a consistent, minimal, and fast preamble that can be dropped into new solutions without rethinking basic utilities each time.

name: Type And Layout Tightening
description: Refactor solutions to keep the algorithm but aggressively tighten numeric types, memory layout, and per-iteration work. Replace oversized arrays, generic geometry, and long double / 64-bit arithmetic with problem-appropriate types and closed-form or precomputed math. Aim to keep asymptotic complexity while substantially reducing constant factors, improving cache locality, and eliminating unnecessary floating-point
triggers: Code uses long double or std::complex<long double> while required precision is around 1e-8..1e-10 and coordinates or distances are moderate.
All problem constraints fit comfortably in 32-bit int but the implementation uses long long for loop indices, counters, and small values in hot paths.
Large static arrays are sized with loose upper bounds (e.g., 1000x1000, 31^3, or hard-coded MASK) and fully cleared each test, while actual constraints are much smaller.
Heavy floating-point loops approximate a clear mathematical pattern (geometric series, binomial probabilities, expected attempts) that suggests a closed-form or precomputable expression.
Graph or DP state uses unnecessarily wide or complex payloads (nested pairs, chars misused for indices, redundant dimensions like prev that do not affect transitions).

Geometry-heavy code spends most time in generic primitives (cross, ccw, std::vector segments, complex arithmetic) although the specific task is low-dimensional or structured (e.g., piecewise-linear in x).
Bitmask DP or inclusion–exclusion enumerations use long long, repeated gcd/lcm, or extra sorts inside 2^m loops where m ≤ 20.
Per-test arrays are zero-initialized with = {0} or cleared via double nested loops even when only the first n or m entries are used.

name: Iterative Linear DPAnd Traversal Refactor
description: Reusable optimization pattern distilled from weighted traces.
triggers: Top-down recursive DP f(i) with memoization where transitions only reference nearby indices such as i+1, i+2, or i-1, i-2 (classic linear DP patterns).
DP states indexed by a small number of integer parameters (1D or low-dimensional) where dependencies form a simple partial order that can be linearized into nested loops.
Recursive DFS over a tree or DAG with depth potentially proportional to n, especially when n can reach 1e5 or more, causing stack-overflow risk or heavy call overhead.
Large fixed global buffers (e.g., arrays sized to 1e6 or 1e7) clearly exceeding the true constraints inferred from input limits, causing unnecessary memory usage and initialization cost.
Use of std::vector<bool> or other bit-packed containers in hot DP loops, leading to slow proxy access compared to plain arrays.
Use of 64-bit long long for all values when constraints imply 32-bit int is sufficient, or conversely use of int where sums of many terms may overflow 32-bit range.
High profiler samples or visible bottlenecks in recursive DP/DFS functions and their small helpers (e.g., has(), gs()) rather than in the DP transitions themselves.
I/O dominated solutions using unoptimized iostreams (cin/cout) or mixed C and C++ I/O for problems with large linear input where algorithmic complexity is already optimal.

name: Specialized Flow And Matching Optimizer
description: Replace generic or over-provisioned network-flow/LP formulations with specialized max-flow, min-cost-flow, or bipartite-matching routines and cache-friendly data layouts. This operator targets cases where the mathematical structure is flow-like or bipartite but the implementation uses heavyweight abstractions (dense simplex, generic max-flow on inflated graphs, SPFA-based min-cost flow, or heuristic search). It
triggers: A generic max-flow engine (Ford–Fulkerson or Dinic) is used to compute a maximum bipartite matching with unit capacities and no need for general multi-commodity flow.

Bipartite structure is present (two disjoint index ranges, edges only across the partition, cardinality/weight of matching requested) but the code models it as source-left-right-sink max-flow with residual edges.
Min-cost or max-cost flow is implemented with SPFA inside an augmenting-flow loop, with no reduced-cost potentials, on graphs up to a few thousand vertices and tens of thousands of edges.
A dense simplex-based LP solver is used for a small flow-like or circulation problem with integer capacities/costs and clear graph structure.
Global arrays for graph storage are dimensioned for very large MAX_V/MAX_E but only a small prefix of vertices/edges is ever used; memset/clear loops touch the entire bound each test.
Profiling or behavior shows many BFS/DFS passes over large residual networks for small logical graphs, or heavy cache misses due to large Edge structs and scattered adjacency.
Heuristic randomized search or ad-hoc permutations are used to optimize a function that can be interpreted as a closure/min-cut or flow problem (e.g., divisibility or subset-closure constraints).
Ford–Fulkerson with DFS (visited[] per augment, no levels/current-arc) is used with very large capacities, causing strong dependence on flow value F.

name: Tight Dp Layout And State Bounding
description: Refactor dynamic programming and memoization code to keep the same asymptotic complexity but substantially reduce constants and memory usage. This operator focuses on (1) tightening DP state ranges to input-driven or logically minimal bounds, (2) simplifying state representation (e.g., folding visited flags into the DP table, switching to boolean or bit-packed storage when only reachability is needed), (3) using
triggers: DP or memoization tables sized by loose magic constants (e.g., 30020, 101010, 600000) instead of tight bounds derived from input constraints.
Secondary DP dimension grows from sums or unconstrained values even though the logic only needs states up to a small cap (e.g., values beyond 100 have no effect).
Parallel vis[][] (or visited[] arrays) exist with the same dimensions as dp[][] just to track computed states.
Use of 64-bit or long long DP cells where all values are bounded well within 32-bit int, especially with a moderate modulus.
DP states logically represent reachability or boolean flags, but storage uses int/long long instead of bool or bitsets.
Nested DP loops access vector<pair< >> or other AoS structures in tight inner loops, with dynamic push_back during preprocessing.
Very large DP arrays (especially multi-dimensional) cause MLE, paging, or profiler shows most time in memory operations on them.
Use of memset with a non-byte sentinel value on non-char DP arrays to represent INF or uninitialized states.

name: Offline Small Radius Graph Paint
description: Optimize multiple distance-limited updates on an undirected graph ("paint within radius d and later paints override earlier ones") by processing queries offline in reverse, lifting the state space to (vertex, remaining_depth), and pruning via per-vertex or per-(vertex,depth) visitation. Replace per-query BFS/DFS with a single shared traversal over this lifted state space, and use flat adjacency arrays for tight
triggers: Undirected (or simple) graph with up to ~1e5 vertices/edges and up to ~1e5 queries.
Each query applies a radius-limited operation from a source vertex (e.g., color/mark all nodes within distance <= d).
Radius/maximum depth d is small and globally bounded (e.g., d <= 10..20).
Later queries override earlier ones (last-wins semantics), or you need the effect of all queries combined.
Baseline solution performs a BFS/DFS from scratch for every query, leading to O(q * (n + m)) time.
Code repeatedly memset() or reinitializes O(n)-sized arrays (e.g., dist[], visited[]) per query.
Adjacency is stored as vector<vector<int>> or similar STL-heavy structure, and traversal is in very tight loops.
There is a heuristic per-vertex pruning array (like maxDist[u]) but it still allows many repeated traversals.

name: Small Mod Digit DP Rolling And Transition Compression
description: Refactor digit- or remainder-based DP with a small fixed modulus into an iterative rolling-array DP with precomputed transitions and primitive modular arithmetic, eliminating recursion, oversized tables, and heavy abstractions. When the DP states arise from sums of digits in fixed bases with exponentially growing coin values, replace the DP entirely with digit-sum formulas in those bases.
triggers: DP states are (position, remainder mod M) or similar with a very small fixed M (e.g., <= 20).
Large DP table dimensioned as dp[N][M] where N is up to 1e5+ and only adjacent positions depend on each other.
Implementation uses recursion over position with depth proportional to input size, risking stack overflow.
Inner loops repeatedly compute (rem * base + digit) % M with small fixed base and digit range.
A generic modular integer struct or heavy operator overloading is used in tight DP loops.
DP uses 64-bit values where results are always modulo a 32-bit constant (e.g., 1e9+7).
Per-test memset over large dp[N][M] tables where only a small frontier is needed.
Problem structure is coin-change-like with denominations {1} ∪ {b1^k} ∪ {b2^k} for small integer bases b1, b2, suggesting digit-sum formulas.

name: Eliminate Redundant Grid Buffers And Initialization
description: Reusable optimization pattern distilled from weighted traces.
triggers: Large fixed-size global 2D arrays (e.g., [510][510]) that are never read in the final logic or are only used as transient buffers for printing.
memset or custom ZERO macros called on arrays that do not affect the produced output (no later reads before overwrite).
Initialization loops using hard-coded bounds (e.g., 510) instead of the actual grid dimensions H and W.
Outer loops constructing multiple grid variants (e.g., k in {0,1}) even though only one configuration is eventually printed.

Per-cell formulas using derived parameters (e.g., d computed from constraints) followed by corrective adjustments on specific cells, while a much simpler pattern using fixed constants would satisfy all constraints.
Memory or runtime being unexpectedly high for a task that only needs to print a simple H×W pattern.
Static analysis or compiler warnings about unused global arrays or variables related to grid storage.
